assignments.title: Critical Questions: The Declaration of Sentiments (1848)
assignments.html:
MODULE 3 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: The Declaration of Sentiments (1848)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: the Declaration of Sentiments from the Seneca Falls convention. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. The demand for the vote was the hardest one to win at Seneca Falls, and it passed by a narrow margin. Suppose the convention had left it out and asked only for property rights, jobs, and education. How might the movement have changed, and why?
  2. Why did the writers copy the wording of the Declaration of Independence, and why does that choice matter for how later Americans argued for women's rights?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Report: Jefferson on Slavery in Notes on the State of Virginia
assignments.html:
MODULE 3 · PRIMARY SOURCE REPORT
Primary Source Report: Jefferson on Slavery in Notes on the State of Virginia
16 points · Word document · one turn-in
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Read the excerpt from Thomas Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia, Query XVIII. Then write a response of 250 to 400 words in a Word document that answers both questions below. Use your own words and refer to the source and to the lessons.

  1. Jefferson wrote that slavery corrupts both master and slave and that he trembled for his country, yet he freed almost no one. Why does it matter, for people who read his words later, that a leading founder wrote them?
  2. Suppose Jefferson had used his fame to push for a plan of gradual emancipation in Virginia. What might have happened, and what would have made it hard?

Your teacher will score your report with the rubric attached to this assignment: understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, clarity and precision of expression, and intellectual honesty. Intellectual honesty means telling what the source cannot show or what you are still unsure about.

Name your file LastName_FirstName_JeffersonReport_HIS7, save it in your Optima → History → HIS7_2026-27 folder in OneDrive, and upload it here with Submit Assignment, then File Upload.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Using Find and Replace (Word). Press Ctrl+H to open Find and Replace. Search for "Jefferson" to check that you spelled his name the same way every time.

assignments.title: Critical Questions: Solomon Northup, Twelve Years a Slave
assignments.html:
MODULE 3 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: Solomon Northup, Twelve Years a Slave
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: an excerpt from Solomon Northup's Twelve Years a Slave. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Northup was a free man from New York who was kidnapped and sold in Louisiana. Using his account and the lesson Southerners Crown Cotton King, explain what conditions in the cotton South made buying and selling people so profitable that someone would kidnap a free man.
  2. Suppose cotton had stayed too hard to clean and the cotton gin had never been invented. How might the history of slavery in the South have been different, and what might have stayed the same?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Exercise: Calhoun on Abolition Petitions (1837)
assignments.html:
MODULE 3 · PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Primary Source Exercise: Calhoun on Abolition Petitions (1837)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
❦ ❧ ❦
Instructions

Read the primary source: John C. Calhoun's speech on the reception of abolition petitions, 1837. Then answer both questions in your own words, in four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Calhoun calls slavery a positive good. What events of the early 1830s, described in the lesson Calhoun Casts Vision of Southern Society and the Peculiar Institution, help explain why he and other Southern leaders changed their argument?
  2. Suppose Calhoun had argued for a gradual end to slavery, as Jefferson at least imagined. How might Southern thinking and later compromises have been different, and what might have made that path hard?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

Module 3 Intro: What Did Americans Mean by Progress, and Who Was Included?
3 questions · survey · one attempt

Before you start

This set of work covers Writers and Reformers Work to Define Progress and Jefferson and Madison Grapple with a Troubling Inheritance. If you have not finished Writers and Reformers Work to Define Progress, read it first. Then answer three quick questions. There are no wrong answers. You will come back to the first question when you finish.

Next up is Jefferson and Madison Grapple with a Troubling Inheritance.

questions.text: People in a country can disagree about what "progress" means. Why might a reform that helps one group still leave another group out? Answer in two or three sentences. You will revisit this answer at the end of these lessons.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 2.3 and 3.1
quizzes.description:
MODULE 3 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Writers and Reformers Work to Define Progress and Jefferson and Madison Grapple with a Troubling Inheritance
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
❦ ❧ ❦
Before you start

This quiz covers Writers and Reformers Work to Define Progress and Jefferson and Madison Grapple with a Troubling Inheritance. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Thoreau spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax. Which belief did that action show?

answers.text: A person should openly refuse to obey a law he thinks is unjust and accept the punishment.
A person should never pay any tax.
A government should punish anyone who writes against it.
A person should leave the country instead of protesting.

questions.text: Emerson told readers to trust themselves and nature. How did Hawthorne and Melville differ from him?

answers.text: They thought nature taught nothing.
They agreed with Emerson in every way.
They warned that people are not as perfect as the optimists believed, writing about guilt and pride.
They wanted everyone to move to Walden Pond.

questions.text: Most utopian communities, such as Brook Farm, did not last. Which reason from the lesson explains why?

answers.text: Congress passed a law against them.
They were burned down by neighbors.
Their members all wanted to be preachers.
Sharing everything is hard when people have different goals and work habits, and a community that cannot feed itself cannot stay together.

questions.text: The Declaration of Sentiments copied the language of the Declaration of Independence. What was the best reason for that choice?

answers.text: The writers had no ideas of their own.
It argued that "all men and women are created equal" and listed wrongs the way the colonists had, so the nation's own promise could be used for women.
It showed that women had signed the first Declaration.
It was required by Congress.

questions.text: Horace Mann pushed for free common schools. What was his main reason?

answers.text: He wanted to end all private schools.
He wanted to make wealthy families pay for every school.
He believed a republic needs educated citizens, and that rich and poor children learning side by side would grow up to be better citizens.
He wanted to train workers only for the Lowell mills.

questions.text: Which pair of facts led many founders to hope that slavery might fade away on its own?

answers.text: Tobacco prices were rising and Congress had just banned all slavery.
Most Northern states had already ended slavery and the South agreed to do the same.
The Northwest Ordinance applied to Virginia and the Constitution banned the slave trade immediately.
Tobacco was wearing out Virginia's soil, and Congress could end the slave trade in 1808.

questions.text: Jefferson wrote that "we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go." What did he mean?

answers.text: Slavery was wrong, but he could see no safe way to end it.
He was afraid of animals on his farm.
He thought slavery would end soon without any action.
He believed Northern states should be forced to take slaves.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 3.2 and 3.3
quizzes.description:
MODULE 3 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Southerners Crown Cotton King and Calhoun Casts Vision of Southern Society and the Peculiar Institution
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
❦ ❧ ❦
Before you start

This quiz covers Southerners Crown Cotton King and Calhoun Casts Vision of Southern Society and the Peculiar Institution. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Eli Whitney's cotton gin saved labor, yet slavery grew after it was invented. What best explains this?

answers.text: The gin broke often and needed many workers to repair it.
The gin cleaned the cotton, but planting and picking were still done by hand, and cotton became so profitable that planters wanted more land and more slave workers.
The gin was too expensive, so planters bought more slaves instead.
Congress required every planter to own a gin and a slave.

questions.text: Congress banned the import of slaves from Africa in 1808, yet about a million slaves were sold or moved within the country by 1860. What best explains this?

answers.text: Slaves were moved because Congress ordered them to move.
Slaves were sold mainly to Northern factories.
Slaves were moved because of the end of cotton farming.
Demand for workers in the new cotton lands was growing, while Virginia and Maryland had more slaves than their farms needed.

questions.text: Which fact shows that the cotton economy did not belong to the South alone?

answers.text: Northern banks, shippers, and insurance companies took part in the cotton trade, and Northern and British mills bought the cotton.
Cotton was never grown in Florida.
Northern states passed laws forbidding the use of cotton.
Only Southern mills made cloth.

questions.text: What was one main effect of Nat Turner's revolt on Southern law?

answers.text: Virginia ended slavery within a year.
Southern states made it easier to teach slaves to read.
Fear led many Southern states to pass harsher laws, such as making it a crime to teach slaves to read.
Northern states agreed to return all runaways at once.

questions.text: Once Southern leaders began calling slavery a positive good, why did compromise with the North get harder?

answers.text: Earlier compromises treated slavery as a tolerated evil that would fade, and now compromise would mean protecting something the South called good and permanent.
The North no longer cared about slavery.
Congress lost the power to make compromises.
The South had stopped sending senators to Washington.

questions.text: John Quincy Adams fought the gag rule for eight years. Why did the rule make some Northerners worry about their own freedoms?

answers.text: It required Northerners to keep slaves.
It blocked the right of petition, which the First Amendment protects, and not only for abolitionists.
It ended the House of Representatives.
It took away the vote from Northern citizens.

questions.text: Which statement from Calhoun's argument is an opinion rather than a fact that can be checked?

answers.text: Calhoun gave a Senate speech on February 6, 1837.
Southerners adopted many of Calhoun's arguments.
Slaves in the South were better off than factory workers in the North.
Slavery was part of the economies of many ancient civilizations.

discussions.title: Discussion: Jefferson's Dilemma, Holding "a Wolf by the Ear"
discussions.html:
MODULE 3 · DISCUSSION
Discussion: Jefferson's Dilemma, Holding "a Wolf by the Ear"
10 points · written post and one reply · threaded discussion
❦ ❧ ❦
The prompt

Jefferson called slavery "a wolf by the ear": wrong to hold, but dangerous to let go. Historians disagree about whether Jefferson and Madison could have found a safe way to end slavery, or whether they simply did not try hard enough. Make one specific claim about which view the evidence supports better. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: Discussion: Calhoun's "Positive Good," Why Did the South's Argument Change?
discussions.html:
MODULE 3 · DISCUSSION
Discussion: Calhoun's "Positive Good," Why Did the South's Argument Change?
10 points · written post and one reply · threaded discussion
❦ ❧ ❦
The prompt

In Jefferson's time many Southern leaders called slavery a wrong they did not know how to end. By the 1830s Calhoun called it a positive good. Make one specific claim about which cause mattered most in that change: the profits of cotton, the fear after Nat Turner's revolt, the growth of the abolitionist movement, or something else. Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
